title: Anybody know any good tutorial s on tutorial s?

posts.author: PersistentDreamerGames
posts.body:
The nature of Googling stuff makes it difficult to look up stuff on how to make a good tutorial, because typing the word "tutorial" pulls up tutorials on all sorts of stuff, but it's harder to find stuff on how to make a good tutorial in RPGMAKER.
Part of this is a question more from a design standpoint. How, in general, do you make a tutorial that is engaging and not overly preachy? I've considered a tutorial building characters can enter, in game books, or a hard and fast battle tutorial.
What are some other good options for types of tutorials?
On the topic of battle tutorials specifically, I have a second question: How would I do that?
I know I can put in text and stuff using troop events and the like, but you know how tutorials make it so the player can only select one option in a battle, the option they're trying to teach you in a battle? How would I go about implementing something like that?
Like say I'm teaching attack. "Hit the attack button" and all the other options are greyed out until the player hits it. That sort of thing.

posts.author: BlackGoldSaw
posts.body:
Having created a battle tutorial myself, the simple method is to use States. Simply create States that seal whichever options you don't want useable each turn.
EXAMPLE:
State 1 -> Seal MAGIC, Seal SPECIAL, Seal GUARD (Use only ATTACK that turn)
State 2 -> Seal ATTACK, Seal SPECIAL, Seal GUARD (Use only MAGIC that turn)
State 3 -> Seal ATTACK, Seal MAGIC, Seal GUARD (Use only SPECIAL that turn)
State 4 -> Seal ATTACK, Seal MAGIC, Seal SPECIAL (Use only Guard that turn)
State 5 -> Add SKILL Ultima (Harold can cast Ultima on this turn)
In your Troop Event you create pages to run each turn adding and removing the necessary State from the Actor. You can use this process to force the enemy to do whatever you want them to do each turn as well.

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
PersistentDreamerGames said:
you know how tutorials make it so the player can only select one option in a battle, the option they're trying to teach you in a battle? How would I go about implementing something like that?
Click to expand...
BlackGoldSaw gave you the answer, but I'm going to say the same thing a bunch of people say any time these threads come up: please don't.
For anyone who has ever played a freaking video game, that stuff is an annoying waste of time, being forced to click/select specific things.
For anyone who has never played a video game but has double-digit IQ, they should be able to read the instructions/descriptions on the screen and either click what they're told if they need help figuring it out, or go "Okay, I read it and understand, I'm gonna just play."
You do what appeals to you, of course, but I'm at the point where if I'm trying a game and it does stuff like that, I return it.

posts.author: Robro33
posts.body:
PersistentDreamerGames said:
I know I can put in text and stuff using troop events and the like, but you know how tutorials make it so the player can only select one option in a battle, the option they're trying to teach you in a battle? How would I go about implementing something like that?
Click to expand...
you can seal everything but attack and use troop events to apply it, but the player doesnt really learn anything from that.
I let my tutorials explain what they need to explain, provide a way that can be used to deal with the presented situation, and if theyre "vital", they cant be passed without using *some* method of handling the mechanics they bring up. I exaggerate effects within those ones so that RNG cant cause a failure while doing it "right"
Spoiler:
Example
the first vital one you get is against a person the MC knows and they join immediately afterwards. you are alone, had no ability to have gained any exp or gear at that point, and arent allowed to change classes until afterwards. Because of this, your skill list and stats are fixed. the player also starts with one item to cure blindness, and curative items cannot be used unless they will have an effect on the target (STB battle system, actions are decided as the battler's turns come up). The "enemy" has negative evasion, max accuracy, negative crit rate, and max crit evasion. the stats and available skills as they are at that point means that the player wins after dealing 4 hits and loses after taking 5.
the point of that tutorial is to show off how her first personal special works by having her use it as an enemy, and then to show the impact status ailments can have.
It starts as a forced ambush and she gets a free hit in on the player. Shes naturally faster than the player, so next turn she goes first and uses her special to enter a stealth state. Normally, her special increases her physical evasion by +75%, guarantees magic hits her, increases her state rates to most magical ailments by x140%, and only ends after taking a hit. but for tutorial's sake, her special additionally has her gain 100% evasion and maxes her state rate for shock. after she uses the special, the main character recalls the trick and thinks to himself that a cast of the lightning magic his starting class has should do the trick and open her up. in this case, it will stun her for a turn.
When she recovers, she then goes second that turn and uses a modified skill from the class she's on to be on to apply an unavoidable blind to the player that is visually identical to the standard one. It guarantees that all attacks miss while active and the MC remembers that they have an item for blindness somewhere in his pouch.
The following turn, shes acts first as normal and starts a charged skill. The MC recognizes by the sound alone that she's setting for up a knife throw and thinks to himself that with her usual aim, there's no way he'd be able to react and dodge it while blind. But, if he could see the throw, he'd be able to dodge it with ease or that that if he braces himself for it, he could deflect the attack as he knows where she'd likely aim.
at that point, either defending or using the item or defending nullifies the attack entirely, but If defending was chosen, the player is still blinded for one turn. Doing neither will either KO the player if they wasted turns during stealth portion, or will nearly KO the player outright if they didnt, but sets a bleed on them that will KO them the next turn.
After that, she's out of tricks and just attacks for the remainder of the tutorial. the player has:
3 turns to land 2 attacks at if they shocked her during that first turn, attacked while she was stunned, and used the item
2 turns for 2 attacks if they made one "mistake" (not shocking her while stealthed, not attacking her while stunned, not using the item while the throw is being prepared)
has already lost if they made more mistakes than that
Failure means you have to repeat the tutorial.

posts.author: gstv87
posts.body:
PersistentDreamerGames said:
How, in general, do you make a tutorial that is engaging and not overly preachy?
Click to expand...
I made my tutorial scenario optional.
first NPC you meet, he tells you to go forward or sideways if you want to skip the basics.
you *get* to the NPC by *moving*, with the *keys*, that you must have pressed to *enter* the scenario, from the menu.
so, if you do *get* to the NPC, I'm assuming you know how to work a keyboard, and how to read.
and if you choose to go sideways and past the basics, there's another NPC that tells you "this is the advanced tutorial... you wanna go back?", "No? great, let's continue."
if you want to take the basic tutorial, you must get to the NPCs that start it, so movement is given for granted.
action, on the other hand, is not.... it's taught right after you understand movement, by changing from bumping into NPCs to actually triggering action.
using menus and battling is just more advanced combinations of that: you scroll with the movement keys, and activate skills with the action key.
everything else, is *mastery of the game*, not *basic knowledge of computers*

posts.author: TeiRaven
posts.body:
I once heard that if there are ten thousand people born every day, then every day there are ten thousand people who are learning for the first time about something that "everybody knows."
We were actually floored, with Inn Need, that we had people saying that they didn't understand the controls. Caveats: we used an engine old enough to vote (no native mouse support), and most of those confused players were new to RPG Maker games in general. But even so, we never expected to have to say "use the arrow keys to move." And then we did, because we had people trying to use the mouse, trying to use WASD, and with absolutely no clue that they needed Enter or Space to select and interact and Escape to get to the menu. So there
is
the chance that yours will be someone's first RPG Maker game--though the built-in mouse support and easy access to customizable control options in current engines probably goes a long way to solving the "unfamiliar controls" issue XD
In FFXIV, the first thing you do is get off the carriage in your starting city, and an NPC calls you over. This means you have to move. That was a real, actual challenge for me when I started playing! Controllers were a very unfamiliar creature and mouse/keyboard was exponentially worse, so having to walk from NPC to NPC to progress was actually helpful. Now that I'm familiar with the controls, of course I find that a little tedious on a new character. But to a brand-new player, it was helpful. Same with all of the Active Help windows that explain things like your job gauges, how mounts work, what collectibles are, etc. etc. etc. You can turn them off if you don't want to see them, but for a newbie? They're a blessing. The Hall of the Novice, where you learn how parties work? A godsend for someone who's never played an MMO before.
All that said, on the whole, I would say that "skippable" is the best type of tutorial. We added a skippable tutorial to Inn Need (or we will have, once we've finished the last* round of final (final2-finalreal-actual-THIS-ONE1) polish XD) that has a little, relevant story to it--but it's not so relevant that you'll feel you missed out if you don't play it. It doesn't give you any advantage in the main portion of the game. But if you're new to RPG Maker games, or to games in general even, it will introduce you to those things that "everybody knows."
If you're going to have an unskippable tutorial section, I think it's really important to not just confront the player with a bunch of long textboxes and/or railroad them into actions. Design a level that naturally builds the player's skill. Use the environment, use character interactions. If there are no other characters to bounce off of, let the player character talk to themselves.  For example, there was one chapter in Fire Emblem--I think it was Path of Radiance? Could've been Radiant Dawn--where the blacksmith and shopkeeper are discussing what is basically their off-screen D&D game. One of them describes to the commander the fictional battlefield scenario, and the commander explains how he would approach it. If you're paying attention, that's the hint for the upcoming map--it's tutorial-ish, but presented in a fun, humorous way.

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
I'm going against the grain here and say skipable tutorials suck(what I mean by that is the usual "This is a tutorial, do you wanna do it?" type stuff). Sure, they're "optional" , but I'm still forced to do them because I can't know ahead of time if there's anything in the game worth a tutorial. I believe the default systems are self-explanatory and don't need one.
Like, did you think about adding a tutorial to navigate the title screen? No? Why not? How is the player ever gonna know what keys to press to navigate?
I'm all for letting the player figure out things on their own. Explain things that are really necessary and skip the other crap. Weaknesses? No tutorial needed. Put some faith in the player that they are able to figure out that a phat "WEAKNESS" popup with a flashy damage number popup means they did something.
Even more basic: Do you really need to explain what "Attack" does? I don't think so, unless your attack command does something wildly different than a regular attack, in which case I wonder why it's the default. And even then, just let the player figure it out. Your early ame enemies are probably gonna be pushovers anyway. They're gonna hit the attack on their volution.
Why would you need to explain Item usage? I'm very sure the player can put 2 and 2 together and figure out that they are able to use items when they click "items". Item descriptions will provide whatever effects the individual items have.
This list goes on and on about all the basic stuff.
Then, if you really want to put up a tutorial for every little thing: Stop explaining everything at once.
The player does not need to be a master at playing your game. They only need the basics and can figure out the rest on their own.
Weakness tutorial: Enemies have elemental weaknesses. Hitting a weakness does double dmg. Done. 1 box and that's it.
Stop explaining how many millions of elements are in your game and what the exact dmg formula is right at the start of the game. It's stupid.
After that, let the player play the game, let them experiment with what they just learned, before dumping the next 20 tutorials on them. You can spread out your tutorial across the whole game. Every time you introduce some new mechanic, have a very brief explanation of the basics and let the player figure out the rest.
I really like how the souls games had their tutorials. Most of us are probably just picking up the controller and push some buttons to figure it out. (Oh my, the player just figuring something out?! Holy moly!) but there are a couple of messages on the floor the player can read. It's just 4-5 one sentence messages too. Just the base controls of the game.
After that, you're all settled. Figure it out on your own. Learn what works best for you.

posts.author: Canned_Dinosaur
posts.body:
IMO, the best tutorials are when you don't realize that you are in a tutorial. The classical example is the first map of Dragon Quest 1: you're in the king's audience room, and in order to proceed you are forced to trial and error with the menu (in those days there was no concept of an "action button") to talk to people, open chests, doors.
For combat mechanics you could have an auto-battle NPC with you that is scripted to show basic strategic stuff, like lowering a target's magic defense before casting a damage spell, or if running away is an integral part of your game, have the NPC suggest to retreat upon encountering a tough enemy, etc...
In-your-face-tutorials should be a last resort. It sometimes can't be avoided like in action heavy games with lots of buttons. But as
@SGHarlekin
says, consider spreading it out. FFVII REMAKE hammered a big chunk of the combat mechanics in the first hour of play. It was a little over the top, and by the time I really needed the mechanics I'd forgotten about them and ended up Googling anyway.

posts.author: TRIDIUM
posts.body:
1: Only ever introduce something if it is relevant. Don't give the combat tutorial if you won't be fighting anyone for another 20 minutes
2: Popups, not message boxes. Don't stop the game. A little window on the side that says "Arrow keys to move" will work wonders
3: Introduce things incrementally. It's a lot easier to build on top of mechanics the player is already familiar with
4: Give a low risk environment  for the player to test stuff out. I know Fromsoft likes to throw a big old boss at you at the start, but that's a luxury they can afford.
5: Know your audience

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
PersistentDreamerGames said:
The thing I'm trying to get a feel for is how to balance the tutorial to maximize helpfulness and minimize annoyance. But different people do have different skill levels and some people just aren't the block of text types.
Click to expand...
Instructions don't have to be a "block" of text. Having a simple Show Text dialogue that appears in the first battle that says "Choose what you want to do for each party member from the list on the left" should be sufficient for anyone.
Of course, I also agree with
@SGHarlekin
that having the word "Attack" there is really self-explanatory. For any other options, reading the description of the skill should also be self-explanatory. You should only need instructions if there's special terminology being used in your skill descriptions.
PersistentDreamerGames said:
So if I don't guide people through it, what do I do instead? I can give people descriptions and the like, but the feedback I've gotten is that pure text stuff isn't always engaging.
Click to expand...
I don't know what you've done or what your game mechanics are, so I can't speak to that; I will comment that instructions don't have to be engaging. They have to be concise and relevant, and then it's up to your players to have the basic ability to focus for ten seconds and read them
But if you're explaining too much at the start, or you have too many mechanics available at the start of the game, then you might want to change that so they're added incrementally over the first area.
PersistentDreamerGames said:
What kind of stuff makes a good tutorial in your opinion?
Click to expand...
I truly think the basic battle commands of Attack/Skill/Items do not need a tutorial.
If someone, even who has never played a video game before, is presented with the battle UI where those are the only words on the screen aside from the actors' names, and they can't figure out they need to select one, they have larger life problems than whether your tutorial is good or not.
If you have more complex mechanics - like the Octopath Break thing, or the spell combinations/cross-class combos from Dragon Age - then you explain them with a concise message. If you feel the need to be fancy, you can use Show Image to show a window that has a picture of iconography or whatever along with its description in text.
Basically, I think even regardless of the possibility that for some player yours is the
very first
video game or even
very first
RPG (which is astronomically unlikely), you still need to have an expectation of basic intelligence and reading comprehension. There's no need to assume someone
could
be an idiot and cater to that
SGHarlekin said:
I'm going against the grain here and say skipable tutorials suck(what I mean by that is the usual "This is a tutorial, do you wanna do it?" type stuff). Sure, they're "optional" , but I'm still forced to do them because I can't know ahead of time if there's anything in the game worth a tutorial.
Click to expand...
It could simply tell you. Like, if the OP truly felt it necessary to explain what Attack/Items do, it could be prefaced by a message that says "Do you want to see the battle tutorial? If you've played an RPG before, you can choose No."

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
By and large, the worst aspects of tutorials I've experienced:
1.  No room for experimentation.  "Here's how you do X!" and you get like 1 or 2 things and that's it.  My first experience with this was the Materia system in Final Fantasy 7, and I've hated it ever since.  The game hands you 3 Materia, which it wants you to equip, shows you how to equip, and then... nothing.  Even worse, the first "upgrade" to this Materia takes something like a hundred battles in the current area to get.  So, the tutorial exists just to teach you how to equip the Materia and that's it.  It's a massive 5 minute dump of information that lets you... EQUIP A MATERIA!  I mean, this is stupid on so many levels.  I have to purchase the Materia I just got if I want more... Let's say I want all 3 party members to be learning Fire at the same time?  I can't do that unless I pay the pretty hefty prices to obtain it that early on in the game.  What if I wanted to equip multiple materia at once on a single person?  Back to having to buy the Materia again.  What happens if I equip two Materia of the same kind on a single person?  Do I learn the skills twice as fast?  No idea, the Tutorial doesn't cover it or let me experiment.  What about this "link" Materia I found?  How does that work?  Oh, I don't get to know because I don't have an appropriate Materia to link to it so that it does something... and even if I did, I'm only given 2 Materia Slots for each person to start with.  Then why was I given a link Materia if I can't experiment with it?
Crafting systems have the same problem.  They don't give you enough materials to experiment with.  They give you enough to craft what the tutorial wants you to craft... and then go find more materials on your own.  But, what if different materials in this recipe do different things?  I can't know until I find different materials to try it out.
Just... ugh.  You need to give me all the tools necessary to EXPLORE WHAT YOUR TUTORIAL TEACHES ME.  If I don't have those tools, then the Tutorial is basically useless to me.  It doesn't teach me anything other than the exceptionally small scope of things you allow.
You know what both of these tutorials taught me in the long run?
"Materia won't matter until I'm like 20 hours into the game when I get more points to level the stuff up, and have access to at least a dozen different Materias and at least half a dozen Materia Slots... so... equip whatever and forget I have it until then (one of the reasons I prefer the Magicite System over Materia as it's just so much better and the way it is introduced and allows experimentation is so much better)." and "Got it, crafting doesn't matter at all in this game."
2.  The Tutorial just showed me something worthless.
"Here's how you do this action!" and that action does less damage than standard Attack... or it takes forever to set up... or that action feels cumbersome to use at any given point...  I tend to have this issue with "Stagger" systems most often.
"Do all this stuff to stagger the enemy, and then you can do a massive amount of damage!".
Ugh... no.  Hold on, let me go grind the low level enemies to the point where I can beat these other enemies without staggering them, because that will feel less tedious than this nonsense.
Anything that is "do all these specific actions so you can fill a guage" make me hate the tutorial for existing, because I will never use this mechanic at all... unless I can't win without doing it... at which point I stop playing the game.
I forget the most recent game I played that had such a mechanic in it...  You had to balance this bar between "too much" and "not enough", so you had to use actions that would lower the bar, and actions that would increase it, so you "keep damage high".  The tutorial explained it fine, but 5 minutes into having to manage that bar, I realized I would never use that system.  I was going to power level as much as the game would let me so that I could ignore the "if the meter is full you take a lot of damage" aspect of the game.  Until I finished the tutorial chapter and the game outright told me, "Yeah, you're only going to get stat increases through equipment and playing the main story".  If only the Tutorial had told me right then and there that I wouldn't be able to get around its onerous and poorly thought out mechanics... I would have been able to quit playing a full hour earlier!
This isn't restricted to just "bars to fill" either.  I've had games teach me something I could do... and it just outright was less efficient than what I had been doing.  Prey comes to mind.  Prey, early on, teaches you that "use the Gloo Gun to slow down and stun the aliens so you can kill them".  It teaches you to use this in combination with the wrench.  I honestly found it more efficient to just shoot them with regular guns... or hurl the thousand grenades I found all over the station at them instead.  I get why it's not as effective as it could be... but it's not effective for very long in the game at all, and then you can ignore it altogether... so the tutorial teaches you something you won't need to use 20 minutes from the tutorial... when you get a gun and can craft insane amounts of ammo for it right away.  Maybe the mechanic is more useful on "hardest difficulty", rather than "Normal", but then... why is the tutorial in here at all?  If it's a mechanic only useful on the highest difficulties, I have trouble understanding why it's taught to anyone at all... since someone attempting the hardest difficulty would be most willing to experiment and try things and have already learned the mechanic on their own without a tutorial.
3.  Tutorial covers obvious stuff.
If a player can figure out what things do by just hitting random buttons... do you really need a tutorial for it?  I get that some people say, "But, they might be new to gaming altogether, so it's useful to those people!".  Yeah, okay.  Maybe.  But, honestly, if you just make the "controls" menu quickly and easily accessible... you don't have to waste time with a tutorial.  If I don't know the controls, hitting "Start" or "Escape" or "Enter" or whatever should be enough to pull up the menu to go into the "controls" section where it tells me what everything does.  The most you need for a tutorial on controls in a game is a popup before the menu that says "Are you new to video games?" and automatically highlight "yes".  Then, any button press other than one which would select a different option (right, down, whatever) would confirm someone is new, and then give them a visual image of the controls on screen and what they do, as well as how often they would be used in the game (here is the Flashlight button, you will need it exactly twice in the game.  Here is the crouch button, you will need it exactly 5 times in the game.  Here is the camera stick, you will use it constantly.  Here's the button for the menu, you will need it every 5 minutes).
Everyone else, familiar with at least one or two video games... will just test buttons to see what things do.
"If you hit an enemy with an element they're weak to, they take more damage!"
Do... do we really need to overtly teach this stuff?  The most you might need to do is teach someone what types of enemies are weak to which elements... and that's only if your combat is basically Pokemon where the only meaningful damage you deal involves stat buffing for 2 or 3 turns before attacking or using an elemental weakness.  You know... where weaknesses are the primary gameplay element.
Even in my own game, where "Elemental Weaknesses" are pretty important, I have no tutorial for it.  I have the gameplay itself lead the player into figuring out those elements on their own... and then have a "book of references" in every weapon shop in case the player wants to check it to be sure.
4.  Tutorial takes away all agency.
Why is this still a thing?  "We can't get started unless you come over here", "You can't move on in combat until you do this thing I want you to do", or the dreaded "here's 6 thousand text boxes that explain a thing to you for 5 minutes".
Look, sometimes you have to take agency from the player.  It's okay.  But, limiting my freedom to do things because "I haven't given you a tutorial on how to do it yet" is really frustrating.  I can't go explore this portion of the world because I have to come talk to you?  What if I'm not ready to start the main quest and want to look around and get a feel for the setting and NPC's and layout of the area first?  Why are you locking me out of areas and forcing me to engage with your Tutorial NPC's?  What if I don't care about the "cool thing" in combat you want to teach me, and want to just mash attack to win instead?  What if I wanted to save my Limit Break that you gave me for a different battle?  No?  Have to use it here?  Ugh... WHY?
It's okay to tell me "Here's the thing I'm trying to teach you" and then let me approach it when I feel comfortable approaching it.  You really don't need to limit my freedom and teach me something.  I'll come learn it when I want to learn it.  I want to do other things first, maybe.
---
Anyway, tl;dr:
If you want to know how to make a good tutorial... just play Portal 1.  Like half of that game is tutorial and you won't even realize it as the player.  It's that good.  Analyze that portion and how the game teaches you the mechanics.  That will teach you how to teach things to your players in your own game.

posts.author: bass2yang
posts.body:
The main goal is to make sure you are not interrupting the flow of the game. Do keep in mind your target audience and remember that time is the most expensive commodity.
Always allow the player the choice of a tutorial if you are including one - keyword - choice. Don't start off the game asking if they want a tutorial at the beginning for RPGs - we're essentially role-playing so put it in the role of the game. Make it be a part of like the training grounds where the NPC captain is looking for recruits and offers free training. Give the player some cool stuff too when they complete it.
Turn it into a player-driven goal rather than a dev-driven goal.
Your players are doing more than just buying your game; they are investing their time to experience your game.
Just... please... do not do this or similar:

posts.author: Avery
posts.body:
One of the best in game tutorials ever is the one from Gothic (both 1 and 2), and they are unskippable.
What makes them so great is that they don't feel like a tutorial. You don't get infodump, noone explains you your controls, no, you start with nothing at a point from which you can only go one way (after the obligatory intro setting up why you are there and so on).
You can then start to loot things that you see as you will be able to do all over the game, meet your first NPCs and learn how to interact by just doing it.
The first enemies are super squishy and you also find your first makeship weapons before that, so you have enough time and wiggle room to figure out what to do.
It all makes sense storywise, it is over quickly, but at no point it feels like a tutorial, it is just your first steps you take on your own in an environment that offers you to try and learn the mechanics before you move into the "real game".
Couldn't find something else without searching to deep, but here you can watch the intro and look into the first gameplay and see how there is no obvious tutorial yet the player learns to play the game:
The English dub is... well... I understand why this game never was successful out of Europe.
